summary: The microscopic build of skin: the epidermal layers and their cells, the junctions that hold keratinocytes together and to the basement membrane, the dermis, and the glands, hair, and nails. Exam questions ask you to name the layer or protein that fails and predict where a blister splits or which disease results.

points: Stratum basale: one row of dividing stem cells on the basement membrane; they make keratins 5 and 14.
Stratum spinosum: cells joined by many desmosomes (the 'spines'); keratins switch to 1 and 10.
Stratum granulosum: keratohyalin granules (profilaggrin) and lamellar bodies that release barrier lipids.
Stratum lucidum: thin clear layer found only in thick skin of the palms and soles.
Stratum corneum: flat dead corneocytes with no nuclei, wrapped in a tough cornified envelope.
notes.why: Keratinocytes are born in the stratum basale and move upward over several weeks, changing their keratin pair and their job at each level. Keratins 5 and 14 give dividing basal cells a flexible scaffold, while keratins 1 and 10 build the dense filament network of maturing cells. In the granulosum, filaggrin bundles these filaments and lamellar bodies secrete lipid between the cells to form the water barrier. The cells then break down their nuclei and organelles in a programmed death, leaving flat corneocytes at the surface.

points: Melanocytes: neural crest origin, sit in the stratum basale, pass melanin in melanosomes to nearby keratinocytes through their dendrites.
Skin color depends on melanosome size, number, and activity; melanocyte numbers are about the same across skin colors.
Langerhans cells: bone marrow origin, mostly in the stratum spinosum, contain tennis-racket Birbeck granules, stain for CD1a and S-100, and carry antigen to lymph nodes.
Merkel cells: in the stratum basale next to nerve endings, act as slowly adapting light touch receptors, plentiful in fingertips.
notes.why: Each resident cell sits where its job requires. Melanocytes in the basal layer push melanosomes up through their dendrites so pigment caps keratinocyte nuclei on the sun-facing side, which is why skin tone reflects melanosome activity more than melanocyte count. Langerhans cells are dendritic antigen-presenting cells that capture antigen in the epidermis and carry it to regional lymph nodes to prime T cells, the sensitization step of allergic contact dermatitis. Merkel cells pair with sensory nerve endings to signal sustained pressure and texture.

notes.h: Cell junctions and the dermal-epidermal junction
points: Desmosome: cell to cell; desmogleins 1 and 3 (cadherins) link to keratin through desmoplakin.
Adherens junction: cell to cell; E-cadherin links to actin through catenins.
Hemidesmosome: cell to basement membrane; BP180 (collagen XVII), BP230, and integrin alpha6 beta4.
Lamina lucida: laminin 332 and collagen XVII anchoring filaments; failure gives junctional epidermolysis bullosa.
Lamina densa: mainly type IV collagen.
Below the lamina densa: type VII collagen anchoring fibrils tie it to the dermis; failure gives dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa or epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (autoantibodies).
Keratin 5 or 14 mutation weakens basal cells themselves, so epidermolysis bullosa simplex splits inside the basal layer.
notes.why: Desmosomes and hemidesmosomes anchor the keratin cytoskeleton to neighboring cells and down to the basement membrane, so the level of a split tells you which protein failed. Antibodies against desmogleins break cell-to-cell adhesion and cause acantholysis inside the epidermis (pemphigus), while antibodies against BP180 or BP230 lift the whole epidermis off the basement membrane (bullous pemphigoid). Inherited defects follow the same top-to-bottom logic: keratin 5 or 14 splits basal cells, laminin 332 or collagen XVII splits the lamina lucida, and type VII collagen splits below the lamina densa and heals with scarring.

points: Papillary dermis: loose connective tissue in the dermal papillae, capillary loops, and Meissner corpuscles (light touch) in hairless skin.
Reticular dermis: dense irregular connective tissue (mostly type I collagen plus elastic fibers), larger vessels, follicles, and glands.
Hypodermis (subcutis): fat lobules and larger vessels; Pacinian corpuscles (vibration, deep pressure) lie in the deep dermis and subcutis.
Free nerve endings (pain, temperature, itch) run in the dermis and reach into the epidermis.
notes.why: The two dermal layers are built for different loads. The papillary dermis interlocks with the epidermal rete ridges, which resists shear and brings capillary loops and Meissner corpuscles close to the avascular epidermis for nutrient diffusion and fine touch. The reticular dermis supplies tensile strength through thick type I collagen bundles and recoil through elastic fibers, and it houses the adnexa. Pacinian corpuscles lie deep because their layered capsules respond to rapid pressure changes and vibration transmitted through the tissue.

points: Eccrine glands: all over the body, most dense on palms, soles, and forehead; watery sweat; sympathetic cholinergic fibers on muscarinic receptors; overactivity is hyperhidrosis.
Apocrine glands: axilla, anogenital skin, and areola; open into hair follicles; active after puberty; odor comes from bacterial breakdown of the secretion.
Sebaceous glands: holocrine (whole cells break down into sebum), open into follicles, driven by androgens, absent on palms and soles; central to acne.
Hair follicle: bulb with matrix cells around the dermal papilla; bulge stem cells sit near the arrector pili insertion; arrector pili is smooth muscle under sympathetic control.

Hair cycle: anagen (growth, years), catagen (regression, weeks), telogen (rest, about 3 months); in telogen effluvium a stressor pushes many hairs into telogen and diffuse shedding starts about 2 to 3 months later.
Nail: the matrix makes the plate, the bed lies under it, and proximal and lateral folds frame it; an ingrown nail is the plate edge piercing the lateral nail fold, usually on the great toe.
notes.why: Eccrine glands are an exception in the sympathetic system: their postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors, which is why anticholinergic drugs stop sweating and blocking acetylcholine release reduces hyperhidrosis. Apocrine and sebaceous glands empty into the hair follicle and become active at puberty under hormonal control, and androgen-driven sebum is the substrate for acne. Hair growth depends on bulb matrix cells dividing in anagen, so a stressor that shifts many follicles into telogen shows up as shedding only after the roughly 3-month resting phase ends.

points: Hyperkeratosis: thick stratum corneum (callus, ichthyosis, psoriasis).
Parakeratosis: nuclei kept in the stratum corneum (psoriasis).
Acanthosis: thick stratum spinosum (psoriasis, seborrheic keratosis).
Spongiosis: fluid between keratinocytes in the epidermis (eczema and acute contact dermatitis).
Acantholysis: keratinocytes lose their connections and separate (pemphigus).
Dyskeratosis: single keratinocytes keratinize early and abnormally (squamous cell carcinoma, Darier disease).
notes.why: Each term names the layer or process that is abnormal, so it points to a mechanism. In psoriasis, keratinocytes divide and rise so fast that they reach the surface with nuclei still present (parakeratosis) and thicken the spinous layer (acanthosis). Spongiosis is edema between keratinocytes that stretches the desmosomes until they stand out as spines, the hallmark of eczematous inflammation. Acantholysis differs because adhesion itself is lost, usually through antibodies against desmogleins, so cells round up and float free.

tricks.text: Epidermal layers from surface to deep: Corneum, Lucidum, Granulosum, Spinosum, Basale.

tricks.label: Desmo versus hemidesmo
tricks.text: A desmosome welds one keratinocyte to the next (pemphigus, split inside the epidermis). A hemidesmosome is half of one, anchoring the basal cell to the basement membrane (pemphigoid, split under the epidermis).

tricks.label: Roof thickness predicts the blister
tricks.text: A split inside the epidermis leaves a thin roof, so blisters are flaccid and break easily. A split under the epidermis leaves the whole epidermis as the roof, so blisters are tense.

highYield: Stratum lucidum is present only in thick skin of the palms and soles.
Birbeck granules and CD1a identify Langerhans cells.
Melanocytes come from neural crest; Langerhans cells come from bone marrow.
Anti-desmoglein 3 gives suprabasal acantholysis with a row of basal cells left on the floor (tombstone pattern) in pemphigus vulgaris.
Anti-BP180 and BP230 give a subepidermal blister with linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane in bullous pemphigoid.
Type VII collagen anchoring fibrils fail in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, so blisters heal with scarring and milia.
Eccrine sweat glands are sympathetic but use acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors.
Telogen effluvium appears about 2 to 3 months after a stressor such as childbirth, high fever, or surgery.
pitfalls: Pemphigus targets desmosomes (inside the epidermis); pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes (below the epidermis).
Spongiosis is fluid between keratinocytes that stay attached; acantholysis is keratinocytes losing their attachments.
Hyperkeratosis is a thick stratum corneum; acanthosis is a thick stratum spinosum.
Apocrine and sebaceous glands open into hair follicles; eccrine glands open straight onto the skin surface.

summary: How the ectoderm splits into surface ectoderm, neuroectoderm, and neural crest, and how the skin and its pigment cells form before birth. Exam questions link a structure to its germ layer and explain newborn skin findings and pigment disorders by where melanoblasts did or did not go.

points: Surface ectoderm: epidermis, hair, nails, sweat, sebaceous, and mammary glands, lens, corneal epithelium, anterior pituitary (Rathke pouch), tooth enamel, inner ear epithelium.
Neuroectoderm (neural tube): brain and spinal cord neurons and glia (except microglia), retina and optic nerve, posterior pituitary, pineal gland.
Neural crest: cells that leave the edges of the neural folds as the tube closes and migrate widely through the embryo.
notes.why: Neurulation divides the ectoderm into three fates. Signals from the notochord and nearby mesoderm induce the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, which folds and closes into the neural tube (neuroectoderm), while ectoderm outside the plate stays as surface ectoderm. Cells at the border between the two undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and migrate away as neural crest. This is why the anterior pituitary (an upgrowth of oral surface ectoderm) and the posterior pituitary (a downgrowth of the diencephalon) have different origins although they sit together.

notes.h: Neural crest derivatives tied to skin and nerves
points: Melanocytes of skin and hair.
Schwann cells, dorsal root ganglia, and sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia.
Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.
Odontoblasts (dentin), while enamel comes from surface ectoderm.
Pia and arachnoid, parafollicular C cells, and most bone and connective tissue of the face.
notes.why: Neural crest cells are multipotent, and their fate is set by the route they take and the signals they meet. Trunk crest that travels dorsolaterally under the surface ectoderm becomes melanocytes, while crest that travels ventrally through the somites forms sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, and adrenal chromaffin cells. Cranial crest also forms mesenchyme that becomes bone, cartilage, and dentin. This shared origin explains why a defect in crest migration or survival can affect pigment, ganglia, and facial structures together.

points: Epidermis everywhere comes from surface ectoderm; the dermis has different sources by region.
Face and front of the neck: neural crest, because cranial neural crest forms most of the facial mesenchyme where there are no somites.
Back: dermatomes of the somites (paraxial mesoderm), which spread under the ectoderm of the back.
Limbs and body wall: lateral plate mesoderm.
notes.why: The dermis forms from whatever mesenchyme lies beneath the surface ectoderm in each region. The head has no somites in front of the occipital region, so cranial neural crest fills that space and forms the facial dermis, bones, and connective tissue. On the back, the dermatome portion of each somite spreads under the ectoderm, while in the limbs and ventral body wall the dermis comes from somatic lateral plate mesoderm. The epidermis above stays surface ectoderm everywhere, so the two layers of skin in one region can have different germ layer origins.

points: Early on, a single layer of surface ectoderm covers the embryo.
In the second month it divides into a basal layer and a surface periderm, a temporary layer that is later shed.
An intermediate layer then forms, and by about the end of the fourth month the epidermis has its adult layers.
Melanoblasts from neural crest move into the epidermis during the first trimester and settle among basal cells.
Hair buds grow down into the dermis from about the third month; mesoderm pushes into the bud end to form the dermal papilla.
Lanugo (fine first hairs) appears around the fifth month and is mostly shed around birth.
Vernix caseosa: whitish coat of sebum, shed periderm and epidermal cells, and hairs that protects fetal skin from amniotic fluid.
notes.why: Fetal skin turns a single cell sheet into a stratified barrier in a set order. The periderm covers the embryo while the basal layer beneath it stratifies, and it is shed into the amniotic fluid once keratinized layers form. Hair forms through signaling between epithelium and mesenchyme: an epidermal bud grows down, mesenchyme condenses at its tip as the dermal papilla, and the papilla then directs hair growth. Sebaceous glands bud from the follicle wall, and their sebum mixed with shed cells makes vernix, which waterproofs the skin during long amniotic exposure.

points: Dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spot): melanocytes stopped in the dermis on their way to the epidermis; deep pigment looks blue-gray; usually lumbosacral; common in darker-skinned and East Asian infants; usually fades in childhood.
Congenital melanocytic nevus: brown nevus cell lesion present at birth, may grow hair; large lesions carry melanoma risk.
Infantile hemangioma: endothelial tumor that is absent or faint at birth, grows fast in the first months, then slowly regresses; GLUT1 positive.
Port-wine stain: capillary malformation present at birth that grows with the child and never regresses; in the V1 face area it can signal Sturge-Weber syndrome.
Dermal melanocytosis can be mistaken for bruising, so it should be documented at birth.
notes.why: Melanin deep in the dermis looks blue-gray because skin scatters shorter blue wavelengths back before they reach deep pigment (the Tyndall effect), so arrested dermal melanocytes give a blue patch while epidermal melanin looks brown. Infantile hemangioma is a true endothelial proliferation, so it grows after birth and then involutes, whereas a port-wine stain is a malformation of mature capillaries that only grows in proportion to the child. In the V1 area, the same malformation can involve the leptomeninges and eye (Sturge-Weber syndrome).

points: Piebaldism: autosomal dominant KIT mutation; melanoblasts fail to migrate or survive, so patches have no melanocytes at all.
Piebaldism pattern: white forelock and white patches on the forehead, ventral trunk, and limbs, present at birth and stable.
Oculocutaneous albinism: autosomal recessive; melanocyte number is normal but melanin synthesis is reduced (tyrosinase deficiency in type 1).
Albinism affects all skin, hair, and eyes, with nystagmus, poor vision, and high skin cancer risk.
notes.why: The two disorders fail at different steps, so they look different. KIT is the receptor for stem cell factor, which melanoblasts need to survive and migrate from the neural crest; in piebaldism they never colonize certain areas, so those patches stay white for life. In albinism the melanocytes arrive normally but cannot make enough melanin, because tyrosinase catalyzes the first steps from tyrosine to DOPA and dopaquinone. Melanin is also needed for normal development of the retina and optic pathways, which is why albinism causes nystagmus and poor vision.

tricks.text: No melanocytes in a white patch means they never arrived (piebaldism) or were destroyed (vitiligo). Normal melanocytes with little pigment means a melanin synthesis defect (albinism).

tricks.label: Deep pigment looks blue
tricks.text: Melanin high in the epidermis looks brown. Melanin deep in the dermis scatters light and looks blue-gray, as in dermal melanocytosis and blue nevi.

tricks.label: Face from crest, back from somites
tricks.text: The face has no somites, so cranial neural crest builds its connective tissue, including the dermis. The back sits over the somites, so its dermis comes from the dermatomes.

highYield: Melanocytes and Schwann cells are neural crest; microglia are mesoderm.
Enamel is surface ectoderm and dentin (odontoblasts) is neural crest.
Anterior pituitary is surface ectoderm; posterior pituitary is neuroectoderm.
Dermal melanocytosis is benign and fades, but it is often confused with bruising in suspected child abuse.
A port-wine stain over the V1 area should prompt evaluation for Sturge-Weber syndrome.
Piebaldism (KIT) shows a white forelock with absent melanocytes from birth; vitiligo is acquired loss of melanocytes.
pitfalls: Infantile hemangioma appears after birth and regresses; port-wine stain is present at birth and persists.
Albinism has normal melanocyte numbers; piebaldism and vitiligo have none in the white areas.
Facial dermis is neural crest, while back dermis is somite dermatome and limb dermis is lateral plate mesoderm.
Vernix caseosa is made of sebum and shed cells; lanugo is the fine fetal hair.

summary: How the plasma membrane is built, how substances cross it, how water follows solutes, and how ion gradients set the resting membrane potential. Exam questions ask you to predict cell volume, membrane potential, and excitability when a pump, channel, or ion concentration changes, including the CFTR defect in cystic fibrosis.

points: Phospholipid bilayer: polar heads face water, fatty acid tails face each other in the middle.
Integral proteins span the bilayer (channels, carriers, pumps, receptors); peripheral proteins attach to one surface.
Glycocalyx: sugar chains on outer glycoproteins and glycolipids; gives a negative surface charge and helps cell recognition.
Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it stiffens the membrane when warm and keeps tails from packing tightly when cold.
Unsaturated fatty acids have cis double bonds that kink the tails, so they increase fluidity; short chains also increase it.
notes.why: The bilayer forms on its own because amphipathic phospholipids hide their hydrophobic tails from water, which makes the core a barrier to ions and polar molecules. Fluidity depends on how tightly the tails pack: cis double bonds kink unsaturated tails and prevent close packing, while cholesterol's rigid ring restrains tail motion when warm and spaces the tails apart when cold. Proteins set in this fluid layer supply the selective channels, carriers, and receptors that the lipid core lacks.

points: Simple diffusion: down the gradient, no carrier, not saturable; rate rises in a straight line with the gradient (O2, CO2, lipid-soluble drugs).
Facilitated diffusion: carrier (GLUT) moves solute down its gradient without ATP; saturable with a maximum rate.
Primary active transport: ATP is used directly to move solutes against a gradient (Na+/K+-ATPase, Ca2+-ATPase, H+/K+-ATPase).
Secondary active transport: one solute rides down the Na+ gradient made by the Na+/K+-ATPase to carry another uphill (SGLT1 moves glucose with Na+ in the intestine).
Endocytosis: membrane folds in to bring in fluid or ligands in vesicles, needs energy (receptor-mediated uptake of LDL by clathrin-coated pits).
notes.why: The key questions are whether a protein is involved and where the energy comes from. A carrier has a limited number of binding sites, so carrier-mediated transport saturates at a maximum rate, which is why glucose spills into the urine once proximal tubule SGLT capacity is exceeded. Secondary active transport spends no ATP itself; it uses the energy stored in the Na+ gradient, so anything that stops the Na+/K+-ATPase eventually stops SGLT1 as well.

points: Each cycle moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, so the pump is electrogenic and adds a few mV of negativity.
The pump keeps intracellular Na+ low, which keeps water out of the cell.
If ATP falls (hypoxia) or the pump is blocked (digoxin), Na+ builds up inside and water follows, so the cell swells.
K+ leaks out and the gradients run down, so the membrane depolarizes.
Cellular swelling (hydropic change) is the earliest sign of reversible hypoxic cell injury.
notes.why: The pump keeps intracellular Na+ low and offsets the osmotic pull of trapped intracellular anions, which keeps water out of the cell. When oxidative phosphorylation fails in hypoxia, ATP falls, the pump slows, and Na+ and water enter, giving reversible hydropic swelling with membrane blebs and swollen mitochondria. As K+ leaks out and Na+ builds up, the gradients that set the resting potential run down and the cell depolarizes. Digoxin uses a milder form of this effect in cardiac myocytes, where higher intracellular Na+ slows Na+/Ca2+ exchange and raises contractility.

points: Osmosis: water moves across a membrane toward the side with more solute particles.
Osmolarity counts all solute particles; normal plasma osmolality is about 285 to 295 mOsm/kg.
Tonicity counts only solutes that cannot cross the cell membrane (effective osmoles), so tonicity decides cell volume.
Isotonic (0.9% NaCl): no change. Hypotonic: water enters and cells swell. Hypertonic: water leaves and cells shrink.
Urea crosses cell membranes freely, so it is an ineffective osmole; red cells in an isosmotic urea solution swell and lyse.
notes.why: Water crosses cell membranes toward the side with more effective solute and keeps moving until the effective osmolality inside and outside is equal. A solute that crosses the membrane soon reaches the same concentration on both sides and exerts no lasting pull, so only solutes that stay out, such as Na+, set tonicity. Urea raises measured osmolality but crosses membranes freely, so an isosmotic urea solution acts like pure water for a cell: urea enters, water follows, and the cell swells and bursts.

points: Nernst equation at body temperature: E = (61 / z) x log([ion outside] / [ion inside]) in mV.
K+ example: outside 4 mmol/L, inside 140 mmol/L gives E(K) of about -94 mV; Na+ (142 outside, 14 inside) gives about +61 mV.
At rest, K+ leak channels make the membrane far more permeable to K+ than to Na+, so the resting potential sits close to E(K).
Goldman equation: the resting potential is a weighted average of each ion's equilibrium potential, weighted by its permeability.
Typical resting values: about -70 mV in neurons and about -90 mV in skeletal and ventricular muscle.
Gibbs-Donnan effect: impermeant negative proteins and phosphates trapped inside pull in cations and push out diffusible anions; the Na+/K+-ATPase keeps the extra osmotic pull from swelling the cell.
notes.why: An ion's equilibrium potential is the voltage at which its electrical force exactly balances its concentration gradient, so its net flow stops. The membrane potential settles nearest the equilibrium potential of the most permeable ion, and at rest that is K+, because K+ leak channels are open while few Na+ channels are. The small Na+ leak pulls the potential slightly above E(K), which is why a neuron sits near -70 mV instead of -94 mV. The Na+/K+-ATPase maintains the gradients over time and adds a small direct electrogenic contribution.

points: Hyperkalemia makes E(K) less negative, so the resting membrane depolarizes.
Mild depolarization first brings the cell closer to threshold, but sustained depolarization closes the inactivation gates of voltage-gated Na+ channels.
With fewer Na+ channels available, nerve and muscle excitability falls: weakness, paralysis, peaked T waves, wide QRS, and arrhythmias.
Hypokalemia makes E(K) more negative and hyperpolarizes the membrane, moving it away from threshold: weakness, flat T waves, and U waves.
notes.why: Because the resting potential tracks E(K), extracellular K+ sets the resting voltage: high K+ shrinks the gradient and depolarizes the cell, and low K+ does the reverse. Voltage-gated Na+ channels have an inactivation gate that closes during sustained depolarization and reopens only after repolarization, so prolonged hyperkalemia leaves fewer channels ready to open. Excitability therefore falls even though the voltage sits closer to threshold, which explains muscle weakness and slowed cardiac conduction with a wide QRS.

notes.h: CFTR in sweat ducts and airways
points: CFTR is a cAMP-regulated, ATP-gated Cl- channel; the common F508del mutation misfolds and is degraded before reaching the membrane.
Sweat gland: the coil makes isotonic sweat, and the duct reabsorbs Cl- through CFTR and Na+ through ENaC to make sweat hypotonic.
In cystic fibrosis the duct cannot reabsorb Cl- (and Na+ follows less), so sweat chloride is 60 mmol/L or higher (under 30 mmol/L makes CF unlikely).
Airway: CFTR secretes Cl- into the lumen; loss of secretion plus more Na+ absorption through ENaC pulls water out of the mucus, so secretions thicken and clearance fails.
notes.why: CFTR is a Cl- channel opened by protein kinase A phosphorylation and ATP binding, and the direction Cl- moves through it depends on the gradient in each tissue. In the sweat duct, Cl- moves from the lumen into the cell through CFTR and Na+ follows through ENaC; the duct wall lets little water through, so this makes sweat hypotonic. In airway epithelium, Cl- moves from the cell into the lumen through CFTR and draws water into the airway surface liquid. Loss of CFTR therefore raises sweat salt but dehydrates airway mucus.

summary: How the hypothalamus holds core temperature near a set point by balancing heat loss and heat production, and what happens when that balance fails. Exam questions separate fever from hyperthermia, heat exhaustion from heat stroke, and explain malignant hyperthermia, hypothermia, and cold injury by mechanism.

points: Core and skin thermoreceptors send input to the hypothalamus, which compares it with a set point near 37 °C (98.6 °F).
Anterior hypothalamus (preoptic area): drives heat loss through skin vasodilation and sweating.
Posterior hypothalamus: drives heat conservation and production through vasoconstriction and shivering.
A lesion of the anterior hypothalamus causes hyperthermia; a lesion of the posterior hypothalamus leaves the person unable to stay warm in cold surroundings.
notes.why: The hypothalamus works as a negative feedback controller. When sensed temperature rises above the set point, warm-sensitive neurons in the preoptic area fire more and drive the heat loss effectors. When temperature falls below it, these neurons fire less and release posterior hypothalamic pathways that trigger sympathetic vasoconstriction and shivering. Damage to one region removes only that half of the response, so the lesion site predicts which temperature extreme the patient cannot handle.

points: Radiation: infrared heat to cooler objects; the largest route at rest in a cool room.
Conduction: direct heat transfer to touching objects or air.
Convection: moving air or water carries away the warmed layer next to the skin; wind and water speed it up.
Evaporation: each gram of sweat that evaporates removes about 0.58 kcal.
When air temperature is above skin temperature, the body gains heat by radiation and conduction, so evaporation is the only way left to lose heat.
High humidity lowers the vapor pressure gradient, so sweat drips off without evaporating and cooling fails.
notes.why: Radiation, conduction, and convection all move heat down a temperature gradient, so they cool the body only while the skin is warmer than its surroundings. Evaporation uses the latent heat of vaporization, so it can still cool the body in a hot environment, but it needs a water vapor gradient between wet skin and air. In humid heat that gradient shrinks, sweat drips off without carrying heat away, and core temperature climbs despite heavy sweating.

points: Sympathetic vasoconstriction of skin vessels (alpha-1) keeps warm blood in the core.
Piloerection by arrector pili muscles traps air; a minor effect in humans.
Shivering: involuntary muscle contraction that can raise heat production several fold.
Thyroid hormone raises basal metabolic rate over days to weeks of cold exposure.

Nonshivering thermogenesis: norepinephrine on beta-3 receptors in brown fat releases fatty acids that open UCP1 (thermogenin), letting protons leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane so energy is released as heat instead of ATP.
Neonates depend on brown fat because they shiver poorly, have a large surface area for their mass, and have little subcutaneous fat.
notes.why: Cold responses either reduce heat loss or increase heat production. Skin vasoconstriction keeps blood in the core so skin and fat act as insulation, and shivering turns muscle ATP use mostly into heat. In brown fat, UCP1 gives protons a path back into the mitochondrial matrix that bypasses ATP synthase, so the energy of the proton gradient is released as heat and electron transport runs fast without being limited by ADP. Newborns lose heat quickly through a high surface area to mass ratio and shiver poorly, so this pathway is their main defense.

points: Fever: microbial products trigger macrophages to release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha (endogenous pyrogens).
These cytokines induce COX-2 in hypothalamic endothelium, and PGE2 raises the set point.
The body now feels cold: vasoconstriction and shivering (chills) raise temperature to the new set point; when the set point falls, sweating and flushing follow.
NSAIDs and acetaminophen block PGE2 synthesis, so they lower fever.
Hyperthermia: set point unchanged, heat gain or production exceeds heat loss (heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, some drugs); antipyretics do not help.
notes.why: Fever is a regulated rise in temperature. Pyrogenic cytokines act at the circumventricular organs near the preoptic area, induce COX-2, and the resulting PGE2 acts on EP3 receptors to raise the set point. Normal body temperature now registers as too cold, so the hypothalamus turns on heat conservation until core temperature reaches the new set point. In hyperthermia the set point is normal and the controller is overwhelmed, so drugs that block PGE2 synthesis have nothing to correct.

points: Heat exhaustion: core temperature usually below 40 °C (104 °F), normal mental status, heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, headache, and volume depletion.
Heat stroke: core temperature above 40 °C (104 °F) with CNS dysfunction (confusion, seizures, coma).
Classic heat stroke: older adults or the chronically ill during heat waves, worse with anticholinergics or diuretics; develops over days; skin often dry.
Exertional heat stroke: young healthy people during hard exercise in heat; develops over hours; sweating often still present.
Complications: rhabdomyolysis (high CK, myoglobinuria), acute kidney injury, DIC, liver injury, and hyperkalemia.
notes.why: Heat exhaustion is mainly a circulatory problem: sweating and skin vasodilation deplete volume and divert blood to the skin, so cardiac output falls while thermoregulation still works. Heat stroke begins when heat gain overwhelms that system, and temperatures above about 40 °C (104 °F) directly damage proteins, cell membranes, and neurons. Heat also injures endothelium and the gut barrier, letting endotoxin and cytokines drive a systemic inflammatory response and DIC. In exertional cases, overheated muscle breaks down and releases myoglobin and K+, which explains acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia.

points: Usually an autosomal dominant mutation in RYR1, the calcium release channel of skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Triggers: volatile anesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane) and succinylcholine.
Uncontrolled Ca2+ release causes sustained contraction (rigidity, masseter spasm) and huge ATP use.
Rising end-tidal CO2 (hypercarbia) is an early sign, followed by tachycardia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis, and rising temperature.
notes.why: Volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine make the mutant RYR1 channel open too easily and stay open, so Ca2+ floods from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol. Sustained Ca2+ keeps cross-bridges cycling and drives SERCA to pump Ca2+ back, and both processes burn ATP at a huge rate. This hypermetabolism produces CO2 and heat, then lactate as oxygen delivery falls behind, and eventually muscle cells break down and release K+ and myoglobin.

points: Hypothermia: core temperature below 35 °C (95 °F).
Mild (about 32 to 35 °C (89.6 to 95 °F)): shivering, tachycardia, confusion. Below about 32 °C (89.6 °F) shivering stops, and bradycardia and falling consciousness follow.
ECG: Osborn (J) waves, a positive hump where the QRS meets the ST segment; risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole as temperature falls further.
Frostbite: tissue freezes; ice crystals and fluid shifts injure cells, and on rewarming endothelial injury and microvascular thrombosis cause ischemic necrosis.
Perniosis (chilblains): nonfreezing damp cold causes vasospasm and inflammation of small vessels, giving tender red-purple papules on fingers and toes.
notes.why: Cold slows enzymes and ion pumps, which explains the steady fall in heart rate, conduction velocity, and consciousness as core temperature drops. Below about 32 °C (89.6 °F) shivering fails, so heat production falls and cooling speeds up. In frostbite, extracellular ice draws water out of cells and injures them, and rewarming then damages endothelium, which triggers platelet aggregation, thrombosis, and ischemic necrosis. Perniosis involves no freezing; it is an abnormal vasospastic and inflammatory response of small vessels to damp cold above freezing.

summary: The proteins, lipids, vitamins, and minerals that build and protect skin, and the skin signs that appear when one is missing or in excess. Exam questions trace collagen synthesis and vitamin D synthesis, match a rash to a deficiency, read xanthomas as clues to a lipid disorder, and explain porphyria cutanea tarda.

points: Inside the fibroblast: alpha chains with Gly-X-Y repeats are made on the rough ER.
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases add OH groups to proline and lysine; they need vitamin C and Fe2+.
Hydroxylysine is glycosylated, and three chains wind into a triple helix (procollagen).
Outside the cell: procollagen peptidases cut off the end propeptides to make tropocollagen.
Lysyl oxidase, a copper enzyme, cross-links tropocollagen into strong fibrils.

Failed hydroxylation gives scurvy; glycine substitutions in type I collagen block helix formation in osteogenesis imperfecta; failed propeptide cleavage or cross-linking gives some Ehlers-Danlos types and Menkes disease.
notes.why: Hydroxyproline stabilizes the triple helix through hydrogen bonds, and the hydroxylases need ascorbate to keep their iron in the Fe2+ state; without vitamin C the chains cannot form a stable helix and are degraded. Glycine is the only amino acid small enough to fit the center of the helix at every third position, so replacing it disrupts folding of the whole molecule. Lysyl oxidase cross-links give fibrils their tensile strength, so copper deficiency yields fibrils that form but tear easily.

points: Scurvy: perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, easy bruising, and poor wound healing.
Menkes disease: X-linked ATP7A mutation blocks copper transport out of intestinal cells, so lysyl oxidase activity falls.
Menkes findings: brittle, kinky, light-colored hair, low serum copper and ceruloplasmin, weak blood vessels, and neurodegeneration in infant boys.
notes.why: Scurvy findings come from weak, poorly hydroxylated collagen in vessel walls, gums, and healing wounds, so small vessels around hair follicles and in the gums rupture easily. In Menkes disease, ATP7A cannot pump copper out of intestinal cells into the blood, so copper is trapped in the gut and copper enzymes throughout the body run short. Low lysyl oxidase activity weakens vessels and connective tissue, and loss of other copper enzymes, such as cytochrome c oxidase and dopamine beta-hydroxylase, contributes to the neurodegeneration.

points: Pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis (sun-exposed skin, including a necklace on the neck), diarrhea, and dementia.
Niacin can be made from tryptophan, a pathway that needs vitamin B6 and B2.
Corn-based diets: niacin in corn is bound and poorly absorbed, and corn is low in tryptophan.
Hartnup disease: autosomal recessive defect of the neutral amino acid transporter in gut and kidney, so tryptophan is lost.
Carcinoid syndrome: tumor cells divert tryptophan into serotonin.
Isoniazid: depletes vitamin B6, which the tryptophan to niacin pathway needs.
notes.why: Niacin is the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+, so deficiency hits tissues with high turnover and high energy needs: skin, gut lining, and brain. About 60 mg of tryptophan yields 1 mg of niacin, so the body can make its own niacin only when tryptophan supply and the B6- and B2-dependent pathway are intact. Every cause listed here either removes tryptophan (poor diet, Hartnup loss, carcinoid diversion to serotonin) or blocks the pathway (isoniazid depleting B6).

points: Vitamin A: follicular hyperkeratosis (rough bumps around follicles), dry skin, plus night blindness.
Zinc: acrodermatitis enteropathica, with dermatitis around the mouth, anus, and on hands and feet, alopecia, diarrhea, and poor wound healing.
Biotin (raw egg white avidin, long-term antibiotics): dermatitis around the eyes, nose, and mouth, and alopecia.
Riboflavin (B2): angular cheilitis, cheilosis, glossitis.
Essential fatty acids (fat-free parenteral nutrition, fat malabsorption): dry scaly dermatitis and poor wound healing.
notes.why: Each nutrient has a specific job in epithelial renewal, which helps predict the signs. Vitamin A, as retinoic acid, directs epithelial differentiation, so deficiency leads to keratin plugs in follicles and dry, overly keratinized surfaces. Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes and transcription factors in dividing cells, and deficiency shows as dermatitis around the body openings and on the hands and feet with poor wound healing. Biotin is the cofactor for carboxylases, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and essential fatty acids are needed to build barrier lipids, so both deficiencies produce scaly dermatitis.

points: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the epidermis to previtamin D3, which heat converts to cholecalciferol (D3).
Liver 25-hydroxylase makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form measured in blood.
Kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylase (stimulated by PTH and low phosphate) makes active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
Less skin synthesis with dark skin (melanin absorbs UVB), high latitude in winter, sunscreen, covering clothing, and older age.
Long sun exposure does not cause toxicity, because extra previtamin D3 is broken down by UV into inactive products.
notes.why: The skin makes vitamin D by photochemistry, so anything that keeps UVB photons from reaching 7-dehydrocholesterol in the basal and spinous layers lowers production. Cholecalciferol is inactive and needs two hydroxylations: the liver step is loosely regulated, while renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is the control point, raised by PTH and low phosphate and suppressed by FGF23 and calcitriol itself. That is why 25-hydroxyvitamin D best reflects body stores, while the active hormone is held near normal until deficiency is advanced.

points: Lamellar bodies in the stratum granulosum release ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids, which form the lipid sheets between corneocytes.
Sebum: mostly triglycerides, wax esters, and squalene; bacterial lipases release free fatty acids from it.
Dermal ground substance: hyaluronic acid (not sulfated, binds lots of water) and dermatan sulfate (the main sulfated GAG of the dermis).
notes.why: The stratum corneum works like bricks and mortar: corneocytes are the bricks and the stacked lipid sheets are the mortar that blocks water loss. Ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids must be present in roughly equal molar amounts to form these ordered layers, so a shortage of any one raises transepidermal water loss. In the dermis, the many negative charges on hyaluronic acid attract cations and water, which makes the ground substance a hydrated gel that resists compression.

points: Most common porphyria; low activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase in the liver, mostly acquired, sometimes inherited.
Uroporphyrins build up, reach the skin, absorb visible light (around 400 nm), and make reactive oxygen species that injure the upper dermis.
Findings: blisters, erosions, fragility, and milia on the backs of the hands, hypertrichosis of the face, and tea-colored urine that fluoresces under a Wood lamp.
Triggers: alcohol, hepatitis C, iron overload (HFE mutations), estrogens, smoking, and HIV.
No acute abdominal or neurologic attacks.
notes.why: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase is the fifth enzyme of heme synthesis, so its failure builds up uroporphyrinogen, which oxidizes to uroporphyrin and circulates to the skin. Porphyrins absorb light near 400 nm and pass the energy to oxygen, creating reactive species that damage the upper dermis and its vessels, which explains fragility and blisters on light-exposed skin. In the acquired form, iron-driven oxidation in hepatocytes makes an inhibitor of the enzyme, a process that alcohol, hepatitis C, and estrogens promote. The block is late in the pathway and does not raise ALA or porphobilinogen, so there are no neurovisceral attacks.

summary: How reactive oxygen species form, what they damage, and how enzymes and non-vitamin antioxidants such as glutathione, ubiquinol, carotenoids, and melanin protect skin. Exam questions connect UV light to DNA damage and photoaging and explain why chronic granulomatous disease brings infections with catalase-positive organisms.

points: Superoxide (O2 radical anion): one-electron reduction of O2, from electron leak in mitochondrial complexes I and III and from NADPH oxidase in phagocytes.
Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2): made when superoxide dismutase converts superoxide; a weak oxidant that crosses membranes easily.
Hydroxyl radical: the most reactive; made by the Fenton reaction (Fe2+ plus H2O2) and by ionizing radiation splitting water.
UV light, especially UVA, excites photosensitizers in skin that pass energy to oxygen and make reactive species.
notes.why: Oxygen accepts electrons one at a time, so partial reduction creates a series of damaging intermediates: superoxide, then hydrogen peroxide, then hydroxyl radical. Electrons that escape complexes I and III reduce O2 to superoxide, and phagocytes make it on purpose with NADPH oxidase. Hydrogen peroxide is not a radical, but free Fe2+ splits it in the Fenton reaction to give hydroxyl radical, which reacts with the first molecule it meets. This is why iron overload and ionizing radiation both cause oxidative damage.

points: Membrane lipids: lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids runs as a chain reaction and makes membranes leaky.
Proteins: oxidized side chains, cross-links, and fragmentation lead to misfolding and breakdown.
DNA: strand breaks and oxidized bases such as 8-oxoguanine, which pairs with adenine and causes G to T mutations.
notes.why: Radicals pull a hydrogen atom from the carbon between double bonds in polyunsaturated fatty acids, and each lipid radical reacts with O2 to form a peroxyl radical that attacks the next fatty acid, so one event spreads through the membrane. Protein oxidation changes shape and activity and marks proteins for breakdown by the proteasome. In DNA, 8-oxoguanine pairs with adenine during replication, so an unrepaired lesion becomes a G:C to T:A transversion.

points: Superoxide dismutase turns superoxide into H2O2 and O2: Cu/Zn form in the cytosol, Mn form in mitochondria.
Catalase (peroxisomes) turns H2O2 into water and O2.
Glutathione peroxidase contains selenium (as selenocysteine) and uses reduced glutathione (GSH) to turn H2O2 and lipid peroxides into water and alcohols.
Glutathione reductase regenerates GSH from oxidized glutathione (GSSG) using NADPH.
NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway, whose rate-limiting enzyme is G6PD.
Red cells rely only on this pathway for NADPH, so G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis under oxidant stress (Heinz bodies, bite cells).
notes.why: Detoxification is a two-step relay: superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to H2O2, then catalase or glutathione peroxidase turns H2O2 into water before Fe2+ can make hydroxyl radical. Glutathione peroxidase uses up two GSH for each peroxide it reduces, so it depends on glutathione reductase and NADPH to recycle GSSG. Mature red cells have no mitochondria, so the pentose phosphate pathway is their only NADPH source; when an oxidant drug or infection overwhelms it in G6PD deficiency, hemoglobin oxidizes and precipitates as Heinz bodies.

points: Reduced glutathione: a Glu-Cys-Gly tripeptide whose cysteine thiol gives electrons to neutralize oxidants and serves glutathione peroxidase.
Ubiquinol (reduced coenzyme Q10): fat-soluble, sits in membranes and mitochondria, stops lipid peroxidation, and helps regenerate vitamin E.
Carotenoids such as lycopene: long chains of conjugated double bonds quench singlet oxygen and trap peroxyl radicals; lycopene is not a vitamin A precursor.
Melanin: absorbs and scatters UV light, scavenges radicals, and forms caps over keratinocyte nuclei.
Eumelanin (brown-black) absorbs UV well and quenches radicals; pheomelanin (red-yellow, made with cysteine) protects poorly and can itself generate reactive oxygen species after UV exposure.
notes.why: These molecules protect through different chemistry. Glutathione and ubiquinol donate electrons from a thiol group or a reduced quinone, and both are recycled by enzymes, so a small pool can neutralize many oxidants. Carotenoids take up the excess energy of singlet oxygen through their conjugated double bonds and release it as heat while staying intact. Eumelanin absorbs a broad UV range and dissipates it as heat, while pheomelanin absorbs poorly and acts as a photosensitizer that generates superoxide under UV, which helps explain the higher melanoma risk in red-haired people.

points: UVB (about 280 to 315 nm): mostly absorbed in the epidermis and directly by DNA, forming cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers; causes sunburn.
UVA (about 315 to 400 nm): most of the UV reaching the ground, goes through window glass, reaches the dermis, and damages DNA mainly through reactive oxygen species.
Photoaging: UV-driven reactive oxygen species activate AP-1, which raises matrix metalloproteinases (such as MMP-1) that break down dermal collagen and lowers new collagen synthesis.
Solar elastosis: tangled, thickened abnormal elastic material collects in the upper dermis and looks blue-gray (basophilic) on H&E; clinically yellow, leathery, wrinkled skin.
notes.why: Wavelength sets how deep UV travels and how it injures. Short-wavelength UVB is absorbed directly by DNA bases and links neighboring pyrimidines into dimers that distort the helix; keratinocytes that cannot repair them undergo apoptosis (sunburn cells) and release inflammatory mediators. Longer UVA reaches the dermis, where it acts mainly through photosensitizers and reactive oxygen species. In dermal fibroblasts these species activate AP-1, which induces collagen-degrading MMPs and also suppresses procollagen synthesis, so collagen is broken down faster than it is replaced.

notes.h: Respiratory burst and chronic granulomatous disease
points: Neutrophil NADPH oxidase makes superoxide in the phagolysosome; superoxide dismutase converts it to H2O2.
Myeloperoxidase (blue-green heme enzyme) combines H2O2 with Cl- to make hypochlorous acid (bleach).
Chronic granulomatous disease: defective NADPH oxidase, most often X-linked (gp91phox, CYBB), so no respiratory burst.
Catalase-negative bacteria leave their own H2O2 for the neutrophil's myeloperoxidase to use; catalase-positive organisms destroy it and survive.
Result: recurrent skin and lymph node abscesses and granulomas from S. aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia, Nocardia, and Aspergillus.
Tests: abnormal dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry; nitroblue tetrazolium stays yellow instead of turning blue.
notes.why: The neutrophil kills by turning oxygen into toxic species inside the phagolysosome: NADPH oxidase makes superoxide, superoxide dismutase makes H2O2, and myeloperoxidase turns H2O2 and Cl- into hypochlorous acid. The classic explanation for the infection pattern in chronic granulomatous disease is that the neutrophil can still borrow H2O2 made by catalase-negative bacteria, while catalase-positive organisms destroy their own H2O2 and survive inside the cell. Organisms that persist in phagocytes recruit macrophages and T cells around them, which forms granulomas.

tricks.label: UVA is Aging, UVB is Burning
tricks.text: UVA penetrates deeper and drives photoaging; UVB is absorbed higher up and causes sunburn and direct DNA damage.

tricks.label: Catalase steals the weapon
tricks.text: In chronic granulomatous disease the neutrophil cannot make its own H2O2. Catalase-negative bacteria hand over theirs, so they are killed; catalase-positive organisms break theirs down and survive.

tricks.label: Follow the electrons back to G6PD
tricks.text: H2O2 is cleared by glutathione peroxidase, which uses GSH. GSH is restored by glutathione reductase, which uses NADPH. NADPH comes from G6PD.

highYield: The Fenton reaction (Fe2+ plus H2O2) makes hydroxyl radical, which is why free iron worsens oxidative injury.
Glutathione peroxidase needs selenium; glutathione reductase needs NADPH from G6PD.
Eumelanin protects better than pheomelanin, which can add oxidative stress after UV.

Chronic granulomatous disease brings abscesses with catalase-positive organisms such as S. aureus and Aspergillus.
Myeloperoxidase deficiency is usually mild and leaves the nitroblue tetrazolium test normal.

Chronic granulomatous disease is an NADPH oxidase defect; myeloperoxidase deficiency is a different, milder disorder.
UVB damages DNA directly; UVA works mostly through reactive oxygen species.
Solar elastosis is a dermal change: blue-gray elastic material in the upper dermis below the epidermis.

summary: How cell cycle control, DNA repair, signaling genes, and structural genes explain inherited and sun-induced skin disease. Exam questions link a gene to a tumor or skin finding, read pedigrees for recurrence risk, and explain filaggrin, steroid sulfatase, and MC1R defects by mechanism.

points: Cyclin D with CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb; phosphorylated Rb releases E2F, which turns on genes needed for S phase.
Unphosphorylated Rb holds E2F and keeps the cell in G1.
p16 (CDKN2A) blocks CDK4/6 and keeps Rb active.
DNA damage stabilizes p53, which induces p21 to block CDKs (G1 arrest) and, if damage is too great, triggers apoptosis through BAX.
UV signature mutations are C to T (and CC to TT) changes at sites of two neighboring pyrimidines.
TP53 UV-signature mutations appear early in sun-damaged keratinocytes and drive actinic keratosis and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.
notes.why: Rb is the brake at the restriction point, and phosphorylation by cyclin D with CDK4/6 releases E2F so the cell commits to S phase. p53 senses DNA damage and halts this progression through p21, giving the cell time to repair, or removes the cell by apoptosis. Cytosines inside unrepaired UV-induced pyrimidine dimers readily deaminate, and polymerases place adenine opposite them, which creates the C to T signature. When such a mutation disables TP53, damaged keratinocytes resist apoptosis and expand as clones, the first step toward actinic keratosis and squamous cell carcinoma.

points: Autosomal recessive defect in nucleotide excision repair, which removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as pyrimidine dimers.
Repair steps: recognize the lesion, unwind DNA (TFIIH helicases), cut on both sides, remove a short strand, fill the gap with DNA polymerase, and seal it with ligase.
Findings: severe sunburn or extreme sun sensitivity, freckling in early childhood, dry skin, and eye damage.
Basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma appear in childhood, often before age 10.
Some groups also develop progressive neurologic degeneration.
notes.why: Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions that distort the helix, and pyrimidine dimers are its main UV target. When an XP gene is lost, dimers persist in every sun-exposed cell, so replication past them introduces mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes at a far higher rate than normal. That is why all three major skin cancers appear decades earlier than usual and why sun protection from infancy is central to care.

points: Basal cell carcinoma: loss of PTCH1 frees Smoothened, so hedgehog signaling (GLI) stays on.
Gorlin syndrome (nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome): autosomal dominant germline PTCH1; many basal cell carcinomas at a young age, jaw keratocysts, palmar pits, falx calcification.
BRAF V600E activates MAPK signaling; it is found in most acquired nevi and about half of cutaneous melanomas, so it starts growth but needs more hits for cancer.
NRAS mutations occur in a smaller share of melanomas and in congenital nevi.
Familial melanoma: germline CDKN2A (p16) loss, with many dysplastic nevi and a higher pancreatic cancer risk.
notes.why: Each driver switches on a growth pathway that should be off in a resting cell. PTCH1 normally holds Smoothened inactive until Hedgehog ligand binds PTCH1; when PTCH1 is lost, Smoothened signals constantly and GLI transcription factors drive basal cell proliferation. BRAF V600E and NRAS mutations activate the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, but in a nevus this triggers oncogene-induced senescence, so further hits such as CDKN2A loss are needed for melanoma. A germline CDKN2A mutation leaves only one working copy of p16 in every cell, so a single somatic hit in a melanocyte removes Rb control.

points: Autosomal dominant (NF1, tuberous sclerosis, epidermolysis bullosa simplex): every generation, both sexes, male-to-male transmission possible; affected parent with unaffected partner gives 50% risk per child.
Many NF1 and tuberous sclerosis cases are new mutations with unaffected parents.
Autosomal recessive (oculocutaneous albinism, xeroderma pigmentosum): skips generations, consanguinity raises risk; two carriers give 25% affected, 50% carriers.
An unaffected sibling of a child with an autosomal recessive disease has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier.

X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis): mostly males, no male-to-male transmission; a carrier mother gives 50% of sons affected and 50% of daughters carriers; an affected father gives all daughters carrier status and no affected sons.
notes.why: Pedigree logic rests on how many working copies a person needs. In autosomal dominant disorders one mutant allele is enough, so each child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 risk, and a high new mutation rate means a first case may have unaffected parents. In autosomal recessive disorders both alleles must be mutant, so carriers are healthy and two carrier parents have a 1 in 4 risk per child. An unaffected sibling cannot have the affected genotype, which leaves 2 of the 3 remaining equally likely genotypes as carriers.

points: NF1: chromosome 17; neurofibromin is a Ras GTPase-activating protein, so its loss leaves Ras active.
NF1 skin: six or more café-au-lait macules, axillary and inguinal freckling, cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas; also Lisch nodules and optic glioma.
Tuberous sclerosis: TSC1 (hamartin) and TSC2 (tuberin) form a complex that keeps mTOR off; loss leaves mTOR active and hamartomas grow.
Tuberous sclerosis skin: ash-leaf (hypomelanotic) macules, often the earliest sign and easiest to see with a Wood lamp, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas.
Tuberous sclerosis other organs: cortical tubers and seizures, cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas.
notes.why: Both syndromes lose a brake on growth signaling, so tumors and hamartomas form after a second hit in the remaining allele. Neurofibromin speeds GTP hydrolysis on Ras, so its loss leaves Ras-GTP active and drives Schwann cell proliferation into neurofibromas. Tuberin, stabilized by hamartin, acts as a GTPase-activating protein for Rheb, the activator of mTORC1, so loss of either protein leaves mTOR on and cells grow in size and number. The pigment signs point in opposite directions: café-au-lait macules carry more melanin, while ash-leaf macules carry less.

points: Profilaggrin in keratohyalin granules is cut into filaggrin, which bundles keratin filaments and later breaks down into natural moisturizing factor.
Loss-of-function FLG mutations cause ichthyosis vulgaris: fine white scale on extensor legs, flexures spared, palmar hyperlinearity, keratosis pilaris, and a thin or absent granular layer.
FLG mutations are a major risk factor for atopic dermatitis because a leaky barrier lets allergens in and water out.
X-linked ichthyosis: steroid sulfatase deficiency lets cholesterol sulfate build up in the stratum corneum, so corneocytes do not shed.
X-linked ichthyosis shows large dark brown scales on the trunk and limbs in boys, corneal opacities, and, during the pregnancy, low maternal estriol and prolonged labor.
notes.why: Filaggrin aggregates keratin inside the corneocyte and then breaks down into natural moisturizing factor, which holds water and helps keep the surface acidic; without it the barrier dries and weakens, so allergens and microbes get in. Steroid sulfatase removes sulfate from cholesterol sulfate, which loosens the bonds between corneocytes so they can shed; without it, cells stick together and pile up as scale. The placenta uses the same enzyme to desulfate fetal DHEA sulfate on the way to estriol, which explains low maternal estriol.

points: Alpha-MSH binds MC1R, a Gs-coupled receptor on melanocytes, raising cAMP.
cAMP activates MITF, which turns on tyrosinase and related enzymes to favor eumelanin.
Weak MC1R signaling shifts production to pheomelanin.
MC1R loss-of-function variants give red hair, fair skin, freckles, and poor tanning, with higher melanoma risk.
notes.why: MC1R signaling works as a switch between two pigment types. High cAMP activates protein kinase A and CREB, which induce MITF, and MITF raises tyrosinase and related enzymes so dopaquinone flows toward eumelanin. When MC1R signaling is weak, dopaquinone combines with cysteine to form pheomelanin, which absorbs UV poorly and generates oxidants. MC1R signaling also supports DNA repair in melanocytes, so loss-of-function variants raise melanoma risk beyond what skin color alone predicts.

tricks.label: Gas and brakes
tricks.text: Oncogenes such as BRAF and NRAS are a stuck gas pedal (one hit is enough). Tumor suppressors such as TP53, PTCH1, CDKN2A, NF1, and TSC1/2 are brakes (both copies must fail).

tricks.label: Ras off and mTOR off
tricks.text: Neurofibromin turns Ras off and hamartin-tuberin turns mTOR off. Lose either and the growth signal stays on, so benign tumors appear in skin and nerves.

tricks.label: Fine scale or dirty scale
tricks.text: Fine white scale that spares the flexures in either sex points to filaggrin (ichthyosis vulgaris). Large dark brown scale in a boy points to steroid sulfatase (X-linked ichthyosis).

highYield: UV-signature C to T mutations in TP53 are the earliest step toward actinic keratosis and squamous cell carcinoma.
Xeroderma pigmentosum is a nucleotide excision repair defect with skin cancers in childhood.
PTCH1 loss and hedgehog activation underlie basal cell carcinoma and Gorlin syndrome.
BRAF V600E is common in both benign nevi and melanoma.
Germline CDKN2A (p16) mutation causes familial melanoma with dysplastic nevi and pancreatic cancer risk.
NF1 is on chromosome 17 and neurofibromin is a Ras GTPase-activating protein.
Ash-leaf macules are often the first sign of tuberous sclerosis.
Filaggrin loss raises atopic dermatitis risk; steroid sulfatase loss causes X-linked ichthyosis in boys.
pitfalls: BRAF V600E alone does not mean melanoma; it is also in most acquired nevi.
NF1 lesions are café-au-lait macules (extra pigment); tuberous sclerosis gives ash-leaf macules (less pigment).
In X-linked recessive inheritance an affected father cannot pass the disease to his sons.
Albinism reduces melanin synthesis in normal numbers of melanocytes; MC1R variants keep melanin synthesis going but shift it toward pheomelanin.
